changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The phase-two outbox of a remote BPMS: one entry per operation which may only reach the BPMS after the caller's transaction committed. DEDUP_KEY is what makes a duplicate schedule a no-op: it holds the entry's idempotency key while the entry waits for its dispatch and the entry's own ID once it was dispatched, so the unique constraint spans exactly the operations which are still planned - a repetition after the dispatch is a new operation (see decision 22 of the repository). It is never null, which is what keeps a database treating two nulls as equal out of the picture. IDEMPOTENCY_KEY carries the derived key for whoever reads the table during support and stays readable after the dispatch; its 512 characters stay below MySQL's index key-length limit.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The log of processed task deliveries: what a BPMS repeating a delivery is answered from. The delivery key is the BPMS' identity of the delivery, 512 characters for the same index reason. RECORDED_AT is the moment the handler ran and never moves, because the age of a task left open is measured from it; LAST_SEEN_AT is the moment the BPMS last redelivered that task, and the retention deletes by it, so a task which is still being redelivered keeps its record.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: What the record says about the task it was written for. TASK_ID is the BPMS' identity of that task - what the application receives in a @TaskId parameter and passes back to complete or cancel it - and it is what lets VanillaBP answer from the record which BPMS holds a task, instead of asking every configured one per operation. TASK_CLOSED_AT is written once the application's completion or cancellation reached the BPMS, so a repeated completion is the warned no-op it always was without asking anybody either. Both are nullable: a record written before them knows neither, and is simply not part of an answer. A changeset of its own rather than columns added to the one above, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: What the dispatcher of this table asks on every wake-up. Two indexes and not one, because the two questions filter the same STATUS and order by different columns: an entry waiting for its dispatch is found by NEXT_ATTEMPT_AT, an entry waiting to be deleted by DONE_AT, and one index over both timestamps would serve neither. Measured on PostgreSQL 16 with 200000 rows, the aggregate asking when the next entry is due took 11 to 18 ms as a sequential scan and 0.05 ms with the first of these - and the scan grows with the table while the index does not, which is what decision 19 of the repository forbids a repeated question to do. The same columns serve the selects which pick the due entries up and the delete which ends the retention. A changeset of its own rather than indexes added to the one above, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The index the retention of this table deletes by, which the runtime creates with the table and this changelog did not. An application applying the changelog therefore had the table the runtime builds minus one index, and the hourly delete was a scan growing with everything ever recorded. What the period has to cover is the same either way (see decision 24 of the repository); what differs is what the delete costs.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The index the open tasks of one workflow aggregate are read through. An extension showing what a workflow is waiting for asks that once per screen, and without an index the read walks everything the table ever recorded. Over OUTCOME and TASK_CLOSED_AT, which is what "open" means here: the handler left the task to the application, and no completion of it has reached the BPMS yet. AGGREGATE_ID is not part of it, for the reason the release of an ended workflow ships without an index either - the column holds 1024 characters and an index over it exceeds the key-length limit of MySQL with utf8mb4 and of a DB2 database using 4K pages. An application with very many concurrently open tasks adds one over AGGREGATE_ID itself, prefixed the way its database spells it. Measured on PostgreSQL 16.15 in September 2026, the read took 0.22 ms with 501 concurrently open records, 5.73 ms with 50001 and 34.30 ms with 500001, and the history did not count: the index scan examined the same 501 entries in 0.17 ms whether the table held one million records or two million. So "very many" starts around fifty thousand, and the platform integration's README carries the rest of the numbers. A changeset of its own rather than an index added to the one above, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: What the record says about the place the task came from. BPMN_ELEMENT_ID is the id attribute of the element a modeller wrote, which is what an extension listing the open tasks of a workflow addresses the model by - TASK_DEFINITION carries a job type or a topic instead wherever the model names one, so the two are not the same question. WORKFLOW_ID is the BPMS' own id of the running instance, carried for whoever follows a task into the tooling of that engine; VanillaBP itself addresses a workflow by its aggregate and needs neither column to work. Both are nullable: an adapter which names neither writes nothing there, and so does a record written before the columns existed. Neither is indexed, because nothing reads a record by them. A changeset of its own rather than columns added to the ones above, because those were applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The index the open tasks of ONE workflow of the BPMS are read through. Whenever a BPMS hands the application a job, VanillaBP looks at the other tasks it still believes are open in the same workflow, so this read happens per wake-up rather than per screen an extension builds. WORKFLOW_ID carries an index of its own, unlike AGGREGATE_ID: the column is VARCHAR(255) and stays inside the key-length limit of every database this runs on, the same way TASK_ID does. Measured on PostgreSQL 16.15 in September 2026 against 1.5 million closed records as history, the read by aggregate took 0.107 ms with 503 concurrently open records and 49.975 ms with 500003, while this one answered in about 0.01 ms at every size. The write pays about 8 microseconds per record for it, which is the trade: a record is written once per delivery and this is read once per wake-up. A changeset of its own rather than an index added to the one which created the column, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: Who is dispatching an entry right now, and until when. A poll claims an entry by writing both, and no other poll - on this node or on another one - takes an entry whose lease has not run out. A running dispatch pushes LEASED_UNTIL along in a short write of its own, so an operation which takes longer than the configured distance stays with the node carrying it instead of being dispatched a second time; a node which dies stops pushing, the lease runs out and the next poll takes the entry over. LEASED_BY is what a renewal matches on, which is how a node whose lease was taken over learns that the entry is no longer its own, and what an operator reads to see where an entry is. Both are nullable: an entry nobody holds is held by nobody. This is also what ATTEMPTS stopped carrying - that column now counts the attempts which ended instead of the claims which were made, so a slow dispatch uses up none of 'vanillabp.outbox.block-after-attempts'. Neither column is indexed: the poll reads an entry by STATUS and NEXT_ATTEMPT_AT, which the claim and every renewal move along with the lease, and the lease is read from the rows that index already narrowed down. A changeset of its own rather than columns added to the one which created the table, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: Where the payload of a phase-two call lies while its outbox entry waits. A call which carries one writes a row here in the same transaction which writes the entry, the entry names the row by its REFERENCE, and the dispatch reads it back. A table of its own and not a column of the outbox: the columns of an entry hold identifiers, one of the four stores does not own its table at all (gruelbox), and a call without a payload writes nothing here - see decision 62 of the repository. CREATED_AT is what the housekeeping deletes by, which is how a row written by a process that died before it wrote its entry disappears again.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: How long the oldest entry has been waiting, which the meters of the outbox read once per collection. It is a MIN over CREATED_AT of the waiting entries, so it needs the third index of the shape the two above have: the same STATUS and a moment of its own. Without it the database walks every waiting entry, and that is the number which grows while an application is behind - exactly when somebody is reading the meter. Measured on PostgreSQL 16.15 in September 2026, the answer took 0.17 ms with a backlog of 1000 entries, 1.03 ms with 10000, 28.05 ms with 100000 and 78.15 ms with 500000; with this index it took 0.07 ms at every size, and the write of an entry did not get slower by anything the run-to-run spread could tell apart. A changeset of its own rather than an index added to the one above, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: Which node removes the old rows of an outbox store tonight. The housekeeping of the outbox - the entries whose retention passed and the payloads no entry names - runs in a window at night, and it works out how much fits by measuring what it does. Two nodes doing that at the same time would each measure the other's work, so a node writes its name and the end of the window here and the others leave that store alone until then. One row per store, keyed by the name the store is known under, so a database carrying two outboxes lets two nodes house-keep one each. A table of its own and not a row in the outbox: a claim is neither an entry nor a payload, and one of the four stores does not own its table at all (gruelbox). The claim is not renewed while the work runs, because a window has a known end - see decision 91 of the repository. Neither column is indexed: a row is read by its primary key.
